description:
Team ElectroPulse is a multidisciplinary squad combining hardware systems engineering, embedded electronics, and software design to solve critical human spaceflight challenges. 

Our mission for NASA Space Apps is to design "ElectroPulse OS"—a cyber-physical health monitoring and autonomous clinical decision-support system for astronauts on long-duration Artemis and Mars missions.
summary: Beyond Low Earth Orbit, light-speed communication delays of 5 to 22 minutes eliminate real-time telemedicine with Mission Control, leaving astronauts without immediate clinical support during deep-space emergencies. To address NASA’s Exploration Medical Capability mandate for Artemis and Mars missions, Team ElectroPulse developed P.U.L.S.E. (Predictive Universal Life-support & Somatic Evaluator), an edge-native, zero-dependency autonomous medical intelligence platform. P.U.L.S.E. replaces cluttered telemetry with a cinematic, 3,697-structure 3D human somatic atlas driven by the Stanford OpenJarvis hands-free voice agent. When physiological anomalies or trauma are detected, the system smoothly glides the camera, peels anatomical layers to expose affected tissue, and locks a laser reticle onto the lesion. Crucially, P.U.L.S.E. eliminates synthetic hallucinations by anchoring every clinical intervention in five pure deterministic mathematical engines—solving intracranial pressure biophysics, Borbély circadian sleep fatigue, and microgravity pharmacokinetics in under 10 milliseconds. Calibrated directly on official NASA-STD-3001 flight standards, 17 Human Research Program risks, and 22 active countermeasure studies, P.U.L.S.E. operates completely offline in less than 50 MB of memory on radiation-hardened spacecraft avionics, delivering trusted, life-saving clinical autonomy when Earth is out of reach.
details:
P.U.L.S.E. is an edge-native autonomous medical intelligence system for deep-space missions where communication latency to Earth (5 to 22 minutes) eliminates real-time telemedicine. It replaces cluttered data screens with an interactive 3,697-structure 3D human somatic atlas and hands-free voice co-pilot powered by Stanford OpenJarvis. When an anomaly is detected, the system glides the camera, peels anatomical layers by ghosting bones to glass, dollies into the damaged tissue with a macro zoom, and locks a laser reticle onto the lesion while speaking concise clinical countermeasures aloud.

It operates 100% offline in less than 50 MB RAM on radiation-hardened flight avionics with zero cloud dependence. Crucially, it eliminates AI hallucinations by computing all triage through five deterministic mathematical engines solving fluid biophysics, circadian drift, and pharmacokinetics in under 10 milliseconds.

The intended impact is fulfilling NASA's Exploration Medical Capability Level 5 autonomy mandate for Artemis and Mars missions, with dual-use terrestrial applications in remote wilderness clinics, polar bases, submarines, and battlefield trauma care.

We developed the project using Python 3.10+ (FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy), TypeScript/JavaScript (React 18, Three.js, WebGL shaders), and SQLite for longitudinal medical memory, designed for embedded flight hardware.

Creatively, it translates cinematic holographic trauma interfaces into functional flight reality: in standby it is a clean floating emblem, and upon activation the surrounding UI completely vanishes, leaving the targeted 3D organ floating alone in deep space with precision laser crosshairs.

We accounted for light-speed delay, cephalad fluid shifts causing SANS optic edema, rapid bone demineralization, and secondary neutron radiation cascades, calibrating every countermeasure directly on official NASA-STD-3001 standards and 17 NASA Human Research Program risks
